blocks.c: I got Wen off the desk and we ran for the stair.

Rule: it obeys its own drawings. North-east corner, push bar, opens outward. It was there. It is always there. That building has never once lied about a stair and I have thought a great deal about why.

Eight flights up in the dark with a torch in my teeth. Minus eight. Minus seven. My legs were gone by minus six and Wen — fifty-five years old, thirty-one years on a mop bucket — went past me on the landing without a word.
"Not down here. Try at minus three, there's bleed."
There was bleed. Two bars, at minus three, on the landing where I met her, standing on an upturned mop bucket holding my phone at the ceiling like an idiot.
"Ravi? It's a quarter to five in the—"
"Stop the car. Wherever you are. Pull over now and stop and don't drive into the car park." I was gulping air. "Please. Please, I'll explain everything, just stop the car."
There was a pause, and a click, and the sound of an indicator, and the sound of a car stopping.
"I've stopped," said Mrs. Dalisay. "I'm on Hendry Street. Ravi, what is happening?"
And behind me, from the stair, in the small neat unhurried voice of a clerk who has all the time in the world:
"Hendry Street. Thank you. That is very helpful."
